roots.context: We counted beans, chappals, dots and claps. Now let us think about what counting really is.

deep_truth.truth: Put your chappals by the door. Count them one by one: 8. Now count them in pairs: 4. It is the same chappals, and both answers are right. Why? Before we count, we choose what to call one. One chappal is one. One pair is one too.
deep_truth.habit: We think the number is hiding inside the things, and we just read it off. But we decide what to call one, and then we count.
deep_truth.evidence: In the activity One Heap, Two Answers, you counted the same chappals two ways and got 8 and 4.

three.who_am_i: You are one child. You are also two hands and ten fingers. You can count yourself in many ways, and each way is true.
three.what_is_life: Many living things count in their own way. Bees can count the landmarks on the way to food. Crows can count their own calls.
three.what_is_this_world: A heap of rice does not come in ones. We choose what to call one: one grain, one handful or one bowl.

roots.thread: Every number starts from one. One more makes two. One more makes three. And you can call many things one: one bunch of bananas, one family, one pair of chappals.

teachings.teaching: Thiruvalluvar, the Tamil poet, says that numbers and letters are the two eyes of all who live.
teachings.link: Without counting, 12 beans and 13 beans look the same. Counting lets you see a difference that your eyes alone miss.

teachings.teaching: The Chandogya Upanishad says that in the beginning there was Being alone, one only, without a second.
teachings.link: Counting begins in the same way. It starts with one, and every later number comes from one by adding one more.

teachings.teaching: The Tao Te Ching says: the Tao gives birth to One. One gives birth to Two. Two gives birth to Three. Three gives birth to all things.
teachings.link: This is counting on. Each number comes from the number before it.

science.text: The Pirahã people of the Amazon in Brazil have no number words for exact amounts. Even so, they could match one row of things to another, one to one (Frank and others, 2008). So matching one to one does not need number words.
Do numbers exist by themselves, or only when someone counts? Mathematicians and thinkers still argue about this.

other_view.who: Plato, a Greek thinker who lived about 2,400 years ago, and many mathematicians since
other_view.view: They say numbers are real even if nobody counts. Two things and one more thing make three things, with or without people. They say the chappal heap only shows two different questions: how many chappals, and how many pairs? Each question has one true answer, and people found it. They did not make it.

practice.title: Ten breaths, one at a time
practice.say: Sit still and close your eyes. We will count ten breaths. Breathe in and out, and that is one. Touch one finger to your knee for each breath. If you lose count, smile and start again from one. When you reach ten, open your eyes. Was each breath the same, or was each one different?
practice.kid: Close your eyes. Breathe in and out. That is one. Touch one finger down for each breath. Go on to ten. Was every breath the same?

how_we_found_out.context: How did people find out what counting really needs? This card tells the true story of two scientists who tested very young children.
how_we_found_out.story: For a long time, grown-ups thought that a child who could say 'one, two, three' up to ten could count. In the 1970s an American scientist, Rochel Gelman, watched very young children count small groups of toys. In 1978 she and Randy Gallistel wrote a book that set out what counting needs. The number words must come in the same order every time. Each thing must get one number. And the last number tells how many. In 1990 another scientist, Karen Wynn, tried a simple test with children between two and four years old. She asked each child to hand over a certain number of toys from a pile. Many children who could say the number words well just grabbed a handful. The words did not yet mean exact amounts to them. Wynn found that children learn what 'one' means first, then 'two', then 'three', over many months. Scientists still argue about how much of counting children are born knowing.
how_we_found_out.who: Rochel Gelman and Randy Gallistel, and later Karen Wynn
how_we_found_out.wrong_idea: A child who can say the numbers in order can count. Karen Wynn showed this was wrong in 1990. Children who could say the words often could not hand over an exact number of toys.

Ishango bone: found by Jean de Heinzelin de Braucourt in 1950; age estimates range widely, about 20,000 years is the most cited.

Adi tala: 8 counts kept as clap, little finger, ring finger, middle finger, clap, wave, clap, wave (standard Carnatic practice).
Wiktionary, Tamil pathinonru (eleven): from pathin (ten) and onru (one). Malayalam pathinonnu: compound of ten and one.

playtest: Walked through every flow as a family of two in a flat. The Bean Test uses 13 beans, a pencil line and a coin, and the count comes out 13 every time unless a bean rolls away, so work on a plate or paper. Race to 20 was played in the head with 1, 2 and 4 players: about 7 turns each, nobody can get stuck, and a star square never sends a player onto another star. Fill the Pairs Mat ends in about 7 tosses each. Step minutes add up to each activity's minutes. Facts looked up on the web while writing: the 1995 bee study and the 2024 crow study, the Pirahã study, the 2006 planet vote, Adi tala's eight counts, Thirukkural 392, Chandogya Upanishad 6.2.1, the two maths places, and the Tamil and Malayalam words for eleven. The three videos were confirmed by title and channel only, not watched, so watch each one before showing it. The kolam step assumes dots are counted row by row, which is common practice but was not checked against a written source.
